editorNote: Winter CES closes with competing visions for the home computer: a new 68000 machine, a compatible Commodore, and Nintendo’s gaming proposal.
morningLine: LAS VEGAS — Lower prices, new keyboards and telephone-line play crowd the winter show floor.

lead.headline: Atari challenges Macintosh with a $400–$600 ST family
lead.dek: Jack Tramiel puts a new 68000 computer family against the established names; software and delivery will decide the contest.
body: Atari is taking aim at the price of personal computing. As Winter CES closes January 8, Jack Tramiel’s company is promoting an ST family announced at $400–$600. The demonstrations began over the preceding weekend; the quoted range is an announced computer price, not a complete system already sitting on a dealer’s shelf.

The ST uses Motorola’s MC68000, the processor also found in Apple’s Macintosh. Sharing a processor does not mean sharing a software library. Electronic Arts president Trip Hawkins estimates that 30–50 percent of a Macintosh program might need rewriting for the ST, making publishers’ support a central part of Atari’s wager.

Atari software chief Sigmund Hartmann promises 25–30 software products when the machines reach stores and reports an agreement with Matrix Software. That is a promise of a coming catalog, not a count of packages buyers can take home this week. Retail orders and financing remain important questions alongside the new hardware.

Atari is also announcing XE repackaging and expansion of its 800XL line, with second-quarter shipments planned. The company is therefore courting both established eight-bit users and buyers considering a new architecture. Its rivals have an immediate answer: existing programs and familiar machines still carry considerable weight in the purchasing decision.

stories.headline: Commodore answers with the C128—and a portable proposal
body: Commodore’s C128 offers a different answer to the upgrade question. The Winter CES machine combines 128K RAM, C64 compatibility, CP/M-80 compatibility and an 80-column display capability. For owners with an established library, continuity is a selling point as tangible as additional memory.

An 80-column setup requires a monitor. No confirmed final retail price is established in this issue’s reporting. Commodore is also showing an LCD portable proposal with a 16-line, 80-character display, 32K RAM, 96K ROM and a built-in modem. Word processing, spreadsheet, file manager and BASIC are built in; the target is well under $1,000, but it is a demonstration proposal rather than a machine available to buy.

stories.headline: Nintendo proposes an Advanced Video System for America
body: Nintendo has brought an Advanced Video System proposal to America’s Winter CES, held January 5–8. The display combines console gaming with optional keyboard and tape-drive additions, presenting games as the heart of a broader home system.

The AVS publicity folder documents this show appearance. The displayed design should not be mistaken for a finished American retail launch: neither a verified U.S. sale date nor a price is established. For dealers considering the battered video-game business, Nintendo’s demonstration is a proposal to watch, not a shipment to count.

stories.headline: PlayNet puts C64 board games on the telephone line
body: PlayNet puts familiar board games on the Commodore 64’s telephone connection. Winter CES reporting lists backgammon, checkers, chess, bridge and go among its offerings, alongside electronic mail, CB-style chat and program transfers.

The listed charge is $40 initially plus $6 per month. Those figures do not establish the full cost of a session, since telephone and other usage charges are not specified. The attraction is clear nonetheless: a home computer can find an opponent beyond the living room without requiring an arcade visit.

briefs.headline: MSX exhibitors ask Americans to wait
briefs.summary: Microsoft showed Japanese and Korean MSX computers at Winter CES but no orders were being taken; Ahl reports the official line was to wait until Summer CES. Not a verified U.S. retail launch.

worldAnchor.headline: Washington and Moscow agree to resume nuclear and space arms negotiations
worldAnchor.summary: On January 8 in Geneva, George Shultz reported agreement with Moscow to begin new negotiations covering nuclear and space arms. This is an agreement to negotiate, not an arms-reduction treaty.

bbsNote.headline: 2400 bps needs someone at the other end
bbsNote.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s January 1985 COMPUTE! column contrasts expensive 2400-bps hardware with the better-supported 1200-bps market and identifies hobbyist BBSs as possible early adopters.

posts.text: The column puts 2400-bps units at $800–$1,500 and says the commercial services it discusses—CompuServe, The Source, Delphi and Dow Jones News/Retrieval—do not yet offer 2400-bps access. Attribute this statement to the January column rather than assume it applies to all of 1985.

posts.platform: Hobbyist BBSs, as reported by Arlan R. Levitan
posts.text: Several unnamed manufacturers reportedly were arranging discounted 2400-bps modems for selected bulletin-board operators. No named BBS, sysop or completed rollout is documented; do not invent one.
CES reporting names backgammon, checkers, chess, bridge and go on PlayNet, with a $40 initial fee and $6 monthly service charge. These are editorial source summaries, not recovered user posts.

curiosity.headline: A tiny robot that remembers its shape
curiosity.summary: Toki’s CES biometal robot used a titanium-nickel alloy rather than ordinary miniature motors.
curiosity.detail: Ahl reports that pulse-current heating extended the robot’s joints and cooling restored their earlier shape. Toki also showed a light-driven interface for robots, motors and household appliances. The writer doubted commercial availability; no sale or price is verified.

gadgetWatch.headline: Technics brings CD players to $400
gadgetWatch.summary: Stereo Review’s January 1985 New Products column lists SL-P1 at $400, SL-P2 at $500 and SL-P3 at $600. SL-P1 offers fifteen-step programming; SL-P2 adds wireless remote and headphone volume control; SL-P3 adds advanced cueing. These are same-month magazine product announcements, not verified CES or January 7 launches.

periodAd.headline: SkiWriter II: words meet the modem
periodAd.summary: Ken Skier’s CES demonstration joins word processing with built-in telecommunications for importing online database material. Listed for C64, PC, PCjr and Apple at $69.95.
periodAd.tagline: A software-shelf spotlight from the winter show.

market.headline: A low price still needs programs
market.summary: Atari’s announced ST price range intensifies competition, but retailer commitments, financing and a fresh software catalog remain unsettled. Commodore’s compatibility pitch gives existing C64 owners a different route forward.
